https://www.politico.eu/article/nothing-.text: The center-right European People’s Party won’t rule out voting with the far right to deliver its policy agenda, even as Social Democrats and Liberals increase calls for an ironclad centrist coalition deal, according to Finnish EPP delegation chief Mika Aaltola. “I’m not saying that there should be anything to be ashamed of in our track record. Actually, I’m saying the opposite. We have gotten our content through, and that’s usually rewarded,” Aaltola said at POLITICO’s Brussels Playbook Live event. He added he is against putting up a firewall to keep out far-right forces “because it leads into badly behaving kids on the other side of the fence.” Advertisement Advertisement “We should go beyond that. On some issues, I think that they [the far right] are relatively sane. On some other issues, there’s insanity,” he added, while insisting a majority of votes in Parliament will involve the mainstream parties. Since the 2024 EU election, the EPP has repeatedly passed legislation with support from right-wing and far-right groups, particularly on migration and green policy — topics where the centrist groups have the widest gaps between them — sidelining its traditional centrist and center-left partners. Liberals and Social Democrats are now pushing for binding, coalition-style commitments among the three centrist forces to prevent the EPP from turning to the far right. “We need to step up also our game in the center … if we don’t find compromises within files, we have to find it across files,” said René Repasi, head of the German Social Democrats in the Parliament, who was taking part in the panel debate with Aaltola. “We need to not to dilute everything in compromises, but give everybody their wins, and that is the point: You need to have this in an agreement with a binding governance structure that includes many other members than simply the leaders in order to increase ownership.” However, Aaltola pushed back against the idea, arguing that the Parliament’s political reality is more diverse. “That’s kind of a Soviet election result type of politics, there’s always going to be diversity,” he said. “That’s what democracy is all about, and so we cannot hammer out that coalition agreement that would be millimeter tight, and no voter will buy it from us.” Renew Europe Vice Chair Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy, who was also on the panel, argued that centrist unity is essential to tackle Ukraine, geopolitics, climate change, and the cost-of-living crisis, warning that fights over the far-right firewall are distracting from more pressing concerns for EU citizens. Advertisement Advertisement “I sincerely hope that EPP stops fooling around and comes back to the center where we can concentrate on the real challenges,” he said. He argued that passing positions with the far right weakens Parliament’s hand in negotiations with EU governments over legislation. “Now you see positions being adopted in Parliament, with the extreme right as part of it, that we go into a trilogue [three-way EU talks] and we’re completely, completely being outpaced by Council because they don’t take that position seriously anymore,” he said. “I even heard about Commission proposals that they don’t dare to put on the table because they fear what might happen with the anti-European forces in Parliament.”

https://www.walesonline.co.uk/news/wales.text: There is "no obvious explanation" for the death of a "bubbly, loveable" 12-year-old Welsh judo champion who was found dead in his bedroom, an inquest has heard. "There's nothing to me that provides an explanation for the death," said pathologist Dr Stephen Leadbeatter. On Saturday, September 14, 2024, Marc Jose Aguilar, 12, had been out swimming and had lunch with his father before returning home. He and his brother Morgan Keogh were planning to watch Deadpool and Wolverine but, while he waited for Morgan to finish watching UFC, Marc went up to his bedroom and told his brother to let him know when he was ready to watch the Marvel film. Less than half an hour after he'd last been seen, his sister went into his bedroom to return some shoes but was unable to get in. She tried to force the door but realised it was hitting her brother who was lying on the floor. His mother, Rhian Aguilar, told the inquest at Pontypridd Coroners' Court: "She went up and went to go in the bedroom and shouted: ‘Mum I think there's something wrong with Marc'. She said: ‘He's lying on the floor. I can't get in the room. You need to be quick’." Marc's family found him lying flat just behind the door and struggled to get into the room. His older brother Mr Keogh managed to squeeze into the room and as soon as he saw his brother shouted: "Marc". He said that as he came through the door he saw his brother lying on the floor. When Ms Aguilar managed to get in she said his colour had gone and he didn't look like he was breathing. She said she couldn't lift him because he was a dead weight and described his pupils as being fixed and dilated. Ms Aguilar described how they phoned 999 and managed to move Marc's body onto the landing where they commenced CPR. Following the call to the emergency services, police and paramedics attended their home in Allen Close, St Mellons, Cardiff . In a statement read during the inquest, Ben Seabourne, a critical care practitioner, said despite continued resuscitation there was no evidence of Marc's pulse returning. He was pronounced dead at 5.08pm. Ms Aguilar described her son as bubbly, loveable, and very popular. "He was very popular with his friends in sport and in school . Even the older ones he was popular with," she said. His brother Mr Keogh said he was a "wind-up merchant", who was always funny and pushing the boundaries to play a prank. His family each said they'd noticed nothing unusual or concerning in the days leading up to his death and said he had been preparing for a judo competition he had coming up in Bosnia. At the time of his death, Marc was a year eight pupil at Ysgol Gyfun Gymraeg Bro Edern in Penylan, Cardiff. He was a competitive judo athlete and swam for Cardiff city. Ms Aguilar said Marc had started following a TikTok influencer to "build himself up" when he went to Spain with his aunt in August, but said he reassured her it didn’t consist of weight training and instead consisted more of exercises like sit-ups and press-ups. She said he was very competitive and when he got home he carried on with the training and would complete 15 minutes of exercises and a five-minute run around the block each day. She recalled how he’d described himself as "lucky" during a school exercise the week leading up to his death and said his only concern was about his height. Marc had told his mum he was the smallest in his year and even though he was popular, some boys would say: "All right shorty". She'd reassured him they would ask his consultant about this, which they did. Ms Aguilar said her son was excited about going to Bosnia to compete in judo at the start of November and was also looking forward to going to Poland on a ski trip in December, and Butlins for his birthday in February. Following his death, Marc's phone was examined by Geraint Strakis, a detective constable from South Wales Police . During his examination of the 12-year-old's iPhone, DC Strakis said there were no texts, WhatsApp messages, or Snapchat messages which raised any concerns. His last internet search from 1.35pm on the day he died read: "How much protein is too much protein for a child?" He explained how during September, in the weeks before his death, Marc googled questions about an adrenaline rush six times. He searched: "How do I get adrenaline rush?"; "What causes an adrenaline rush?"; "How do you go through an adrenaline rush?"; "If you go through an adrenaline rush could you go through 100% of your strength?" ; "What happens if a human goes through an adrenaline rush?". Before these searches, on August 21, he searched: "Something weird is happening to my body, like it's in speed motion?" Pathologist Dr Leadbeatter said he hadn't found any significant injury anywhere on Marc's body. "In particular, I didn't find any mark in or on the neck apart from a very small scratch on the left side," he added. Dr Leadbeatter said he found nothing of note during his examination of Marc's organs, no evidence of natural disease, or of an asthma attack, and said there was no defects found in his DNA. He said: "I don't have anything that gives me an obvious explanation for Marc's death. "I can't really give you an explanation of how Marc has come to die.” Coroner Gavin Knox recorded Marc's medical cause of death as pressure to the neck but said he did not think Marc had intended to end his own life, recording a conclusion of misadventure. Mr Knox said the overall circumstances showed an action taken by Marc prior to his death had not been an accident. The coroner added: “I therefore have to find that Marc deliberately applied pressure to his neck." At the time of his death his school said: "It is with great sadness that we announce that one of our pupils passed away suddenly over the weekend. Marc Aguilar of 8 Rhymni 2 was a popular and likeable pupil and a keen sportsman. He had many friends at Bro Edern and he will be missed sorely."

https://mizrahiauctions.com/auction/217-.text: Auction 1 - Rare Hebrew Books, Manuscripts & Rabbinic Letters Lot 136: UNPUBLISHED. 1000+ HAGAHOT OF R. SHABTAI SOFER. SHULHAN ARUKH, ORACH CHAIM. With the glosses of R. Moshe Isserles (Rema). Cracow, 1580. Description The personal working Shulhan Arukh of R. Shabtai Sofer, filled with his handwritten source references to the Rema and extensive scholarly glosses. A remarkable witness to the formation and early transmission of the printed Shulhan Arukh. Few books allow us to look over the shoulder of a seventeenth-century Torah scholar at work. This volume does. R. Shabbetai Sofer was among the distinguished scholars of the generation following the Rema, a disciple of R. Mordekhai Yaffe, the Levush, and a renowned grammarian and expert in the precise text of the prayers. His reputation was such that the Vaad Arba Aratzot, the central governing body of Polish Jewry, entrusted him with the preparation of an authoritative Siddur, a monumental undertaking intended to establish a carefully corrected text of the prayers together with their laws and explanations. His work received the approval of the leading rabbinic authorities of the age, including R. Yehoshua Falk Katz, author of the Sema, and R. Meir of Lublin, the Maharam Lublin. The present volume reveals another side of that same scholar: Shabbetai Sofer at his desk, studying and annotating his personal copy of the Shulhan Arukh. The edition itself is significant. The Rema’s Hagahot had transformed R. Yosef Karo’s code into the authoritative halachic work of Ashkenazic Jewry, yet the early editions offered the reader the Rema’s rulings without the familiar source references that accompany them today. Only in the Cracow edition of 1607 did a systematic apparatus of mareh mekomot appear alongside the Rema, the publishers explicitly announcing that they had supplied references to his sources. Into this earlier 1580 edition, Shabbetai Sofer painstakingly entered by hand a remarkably extensive series of mareh mekomot to the Rema. Their importance becomes apparent upon comparison with the first printed references of 1607. Sofer’s references are extraordinarily close to that apparatus, at times even sharing its peculiar readings, while elsewhere they differ, omit references found in print, or make a printed citation considerably more precise. At OC 426:2, for example, the 1607 edition refers simply to Rabbenu Bahya, Parashat Vayeshev; Sofer supplies the very verse intended, “Vayikra shemo Zerach.” Elsewhere both witnesses preserve the same curious wording, בשביל where later editions corrected the reading to בשם. These are traces of a textual relationship whose precise nature remains to be determined. The question raised by the volume is tantalizing: when, and from what, did Sofer compile these references? The book itself preserves clues to the years in which it remained upon Sofer’s desk. Interspersed with the source references are substantial scholarly glosses in the same hand, and through them an extraordinary picture emerges of the breadth of his learning and of the working library at his disposal. The range extends far beyond the familiar halachic authorities. He cites from R. Shlomo Almoli’s Pitron Halomot; HaParchi’s Kaftor va-Ferach; the Shelah, R. Yeshayah Horowitz, from his notes to his father’s Emek Berakhah; refers to the Maharal of Prague and his Netivot Olam; draws upon the writings of R. Nathan Shapira of Grodno and even makes use of the exceedingly early and unusual Sefer Habakbuk HaNavi, first printed by Gershom Soncino at Pesaro in 1513, a curious Purim composition whose authorship has long been discussed and which has been argued to be the work of the Ralbag. These are no sterile bibliographical citations. The margins preserve Sofer reacting to the religious life around him. He records a rebuke he had personally delivered to the gabbai, R. Mordechai ben Shmuel, who had permitted money collected on Purim for the poor to be diverted toward payment of the chazzan’s wages. Elsewhere, he engages critically with his contemporary and fellow disciple of the Levush, R. Yissachar Ber Eilenburg, author of Be’er Sheva. Occasionally he refers to his own revered teacher, the Levush, as ז״ל, placing that annotation after the Levush’s death (1612), while his citation of a precise folio in the first printed Be’er Sheva places another after its publication in Venice (1614). Across these leaves we encounter Sofer as posek, bibliophile and communal scholar: reading newly published works, remembering conversations and controversies, correcting practice, challenging fellow scholars, and continually adding the fruits of his learning to the Shulchan Aruch he kept before him. Thus the volume appears to have remained a living scholarly instrument in Sofer’s hands for years: an old Shulchan Aruch continually consulted, corrected, supplemented and brought abreast of the Torah literature appearing around him. And its story seems to extend still further. Among its substantial manuscript entries is a moving meditation upon the destruction of Jerusalem, exile, repentance and the coming of Mashiach. The writer reflects upon the signs given by Hazal for the generation of redemption and concludes with an apparent personal memorandum dated by the Messianic chronogram אגל״ה משי״ח (c.1636). The same later hand appears elsewhere in the volume describing the practice of “פה ירושלי׳ תוב״ב” (“here in Jerusalem”). The language is especially evocative in light of Shabbetai Sofer’s presence in Jerusalem at the end of his life, independently documented in 1637. Even the choice of chronogram has a striking parallel in Sofer’s own Siddur: decades earlier he had dated his celebrated “Special Introduction” with the words יב״א משי״ח (c.1611) The handwriting of these later Jerusalem entries differs from that of the principal annotations, as might naturally occur across decades of a man’s life. Yet taken together, the leaves preserve something exceedingly rare: the possibility of following a major seventeenth-century scholar through the changing intellectual landscape of his lifetime, perhaps from Poland to Jerusalem, within the pages of a single book. The scholarly significance of the volume reaches beyond its association with an eminent owner. The authorship and history of the mareh mekomot to the Rema have long attracted attention precisely because those references became an inseparable part of the Shulchan Aruch studied for generations. Early and later poskim recognized that the references were not themselves the words of the Rema and occasionally subjected them to criticism. Here survives an extensive manuscript witness, written by one of the foremost textual scholars of the period, extraordinarily close to the earliest printed apparatus yet possessing readings of its own. Whether Sofer copied and refined the newly printed references, drew upon an earlier common source, or participated in some more complicated chain of transmission remains a subject for further research. The volume preserves the evidence itself. Beyond the bibliographical question lies the book’s more immediate appeal. This is Torah scholarship surviving in the physical object in which it was performed: citations entered beside the Rema, sources checked and amplified, contemporary authorities weighed and sometimes challenged, later thoughts added as the owner’s library and circumstances changed. Five centuries after the volume left the Cracow press, the intellectual life of its learned annotator remains visible across its margins. Physical description and provenance : Cracow, 1580. Orach Chaim only. Title and several leaves with reinforced borders. Punctures to upper margins of pp. 6 and 13, not affecting text; professionally repaired loss affecting text on p. 7; slight marginal tear to p. 86. P. 48 lacking, with a blank leaf bound in its place. Pp. 108–109 lacking and supplied in manuscript on two leaves (four pages), carefully written in two columns with headings and se’if divisions, reproducing the missing Shulchan Aruch and Hagahot Rema. Four additional sides at the conclusion contain substantial manuscript material by Sofer. Paper repairs throughout at times affecting marginalia. A few leaves have some marginalia with some loss on outer margins. Early ownership inscription of Menahem Mendel ben R. Yehiel Michel, appearing both in R. Yosef Karo’s introduction and again at the end of the volume. Later title-page inscription of Yosef Aryeh Kahana. Purple ownership stamp of R. Shmuel (“Shmelke”) Gintzler, Av Beit Din of Oberwischau (Vișeu de Sus, Maramureș), distinguished posek and author of Meshiv Nefesh. The Kahana inscription may reflect a connection with the Kahana family into which R. Gintzler married, although the precise relationship has not been established.
